records.name: Daegu
records.current_summary: Daegu carries the most sustained municipal hostility to a public queer event in South Korea, justifying a −0.07 deviation below the national 0.71. City officials directly clashed with police as municipal workers attempted to prevent Daegu Queer Cultural Festival organisers from setting up at their Jung District venue; the PPP mayor is named as the driver of the obstruction. Police, however, intervened to stop the municipal workers—an institutional response that partly mitigates the threat.  The festival, the second-oldest in Korea (since June 2009), has run every year for 17 years 'without fail… as a form of resistance against hate and discriminatory politics,' including 2025 ('We Will Not Be E(r)ased') and 2026 ('事必Q정'). This persistence signals that municipal obstruction is real but does not prevent the event, and that the recurring annual counter-mobilisation by a Daegu-Gyeongbuk conservative-Protestant umbrella (about 3,500 believers from some 1,600 churches along a 450 m stretch, timed against the festival) creates a high-density confrontational environment for a visible trans visitor during festival season. Outside those specific dates, everyday street risk is comparatively low per the dossier.  Compared to Seoul (0.66): Daegu's hostility is narrower in geographic scale but more directly obstructive to a traveler attending a specific public event. Seoul's 1.1-million megarally is a broader climate signal; Daegu's pattern is a repeated, concentrated interference at one venue every year. Both cities share the PPP-mayor-and-Pride framing; Daegu edges lower because the obstruction targets the event itself rather than surrounding it.

sources.claim: Korea JoongAng Daily (2025): the Daegu Queer Culture Festival — begun June 2009 and second-oldest in Korea after Seoul — announced that year's event under the slogan 'We Will Not Be E(r)ased' on Dongseong-ro's bus-only zone in central Daegu, saying it has taken place every year without fail for 17 years as resistance to hate and discriminatory politics despite interference; organisers cite a Supreme Court ruling on local anti-discrimination ordinances as affirming sexual minorities as citizens protected by the Constitution.

Kidok (Korean Christian daily, September 2025): a Daegu-Gyeongbuk conservative-Protestant umbrella body convened its 17th annual 'National Assembly Against Queer' response to the Daegu Queer Culture Festival, gathering roughly 3,500 believers from about 1,600 churches at Banwoldang station and along a 450 m stretch toward Gyesan intersection under anti-homosexuality slogans.

records.name: Daejeon
records.current_summary: Daejeon presents mixed evidence yielding a −0.02 deviation from the national 0.71. In October 2021 the Daejeon District Court issued Korea's most important pro-trans ruling, ordering cancellation of the Army's forced discharge of transgender soldier Byun Hee-soo and holding that the military should have considered her a woman when assessing fitness for duty—a landmark institutional recognition. In June 2024, after the Ministry of National Defense reversed the Army's 'natural death' classification and recognised her 2021 death as service-related, Byun was buried at the National Cemetery in Daejeon. Approximately 60 activists gathered to protest the burial, a visible public rejection of state recognition of a trans person at the nation's memorial ground.  The court ruling is a positive institutional signal but is historical (2021) and addresses a specific administrative-military dispute rather than establishing general protections; a visitor encounters no ongoing Daejeon-specific legal advantage. The burial protest is traveler-facing (public hostility in an open space) but small in scale (60 people) and non-repeating—per the single-incident rule, it barely moves the score absent pattern. Net: the two findings largely cancel, leaving a small −0.02 below national for the residual negative event in public space. Compared to North Chungcheong (0.69), which shares the Byun case's origin but lacks the positive court ruling, Daejeon's mixed record yields the same deviation from a different direction.

sources.claim: Yonhap (7 October 2021): the Daejeon District Court ordered cancellation of the Army's forced discharge of the deceased transgender soldier Byun Hee-soo, holding that the military should have considered Byun a woman when reviewing fitness for duty — described as a landmark ruling in a suit brought to repeal the discharge decision.

Aju Press (25 June 2024): Byun Hee-soo was laid to rest at the National Cemetery in Daejeon on 24 June 2024 — after the Ministry of National Defense reversed the Army's original classification and recognised the 2021 death as service-related; about 60 activists gathered to protest the burial, arguing her service did not qualify her to be interred there.

records.name: Gyeonggi
records.current_summary: Gyeonggi is scored +0.02 above the national 0.71 on the basis of its role as the origin and continuing custodian of South Korea's student human-rights protections. The model ordinance covering discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity was 'first enacted in 2010 by a progressive superintendent of education for Gyeonggi Province,' was adopted by the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education in 2012, and spread to other offices before the 2024–26 repeal wave. When the Seoul Metropolitan Council - controlled by the conservative People Power Party, acting on a campaign begun by religious and parents' coalitions in August 2022 - abolished Seoul's ordinance on 26 April 2024, Gyeonggi stood among only six regional education offices still enforcing such ordinances (with Gwangju, North Jeolla, South Chungcheong, Incheon and Jeju), and a Gyeonggi teacher was quoted warning that abolishing the ordinance outright 'will bring a regression to human rights in the education sector.'  The deviation is small and the evidence is resident-facing (school non-discrimination rules), carrying limited weight for a traveler per the scoring rules. No Gyeonggi-specific enforcement action, event, incident, or police practice favouring or disfavours a visible trans visitor, and no Gyeonggi council repeal move is on record. (An earlier version of this record credited Gyeonggi's superintendent with blocking Seoul's 2024 repeal; that challenge - the sit-in protest and the July 2024 Supreme Court petition that suspended the abolition - belongs to the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education and its superintendent, not to Gyeonggi. What remains is the origin-and-continued-enforcement record: still the clearest positive sub-national signal in the dossier relative to Seoul (0.66), whose council has twice voted to delete the same ordinance, though its traveler-facing impact remains minimal.)

sources.claim: Korea Times report (28 April 2024) on the Seoul Metropolitan Council's abolition of the Seoul Student Human Rights Ordinance twelve years after the Seoul office adopted it: the ordinance model was 'first enacted in 2010 by a progressive superintendent of education for Gyeonggi Province'; abolition was pushed by the ruling People Power Party council after an August 2022 campaign by religious groups and parents objecting to its sexual-orientation clause; six regional education offices - Gyeonggi, Gwangju, North Jeolla, South Chungcheong, Incheon and Jeju - still enforced comparable ordinances at publication; the (Seoul) superintendent began a sit-in protest against the abolition, and the opposition-led National Assembly said it would legislate a national student-rights act regardless of regional decisions. A quoted Gyeonggi-based teacher defended the ordinance against wholesale abolition.

records.name: Bayern
records.current_summary: A gender-inclusive-language ban has been in force in all Bavarian public administration, schools and universities since 1 April 2024, following a Söder government declaration and cabinet decision. A visitor dealing with any registry office, police station, hospital admission desk or school operates in an environment where official gender-inclusive framing is prohibited — described in the dossier as "pure symbol politics" but practically a standing instruction of institutional hostility at every public counter. Bavaria is also a partner in the Sachsen/Thüringen/Sachsen-Anhalt Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act (SBGG).  Bavarian police recorded 2,021 hate crimes in 2024 (up 8.2 % from 1,867 in 2023), but the LSBTIQ-specific breakdown was contested in a parliamentary query and the dossier cautions that high counts may reflect better police classification rather than greater danger. No documented street-violence incident specific to a trans visitor was found for Bavaria in this pass.  National score is 0.71. Bayern sits 0.04 below: the legislative hostility (SBGG initiative) and the universal administrative-language ban create a uniformly colder official interface for a visitor, without the physical-attack evidence present in Brandenburg (0.66) or the equality-dismantling bill in Thüringen (0.65). The deviation reflects institutional posture rather than demonstrated violence.

sources.claim: Tagesschau report on Bavaria's gender-language ban: from 1 April 2024, gender-inclusive German is prohibited in schools, universities and all state administration, implementing the Söder government declaration of December 2023 and a cabinet decision amending the language rules of public authorities; critics in the coverage dismiss it as symbol politics while noting its practical reach across every public counter, registry office and classroom.

Antenne Bayern report on the Bundesrat initiative by several Länder — Sachsen, Thüringen and Sachsen-Anhalt, with Bavaria a partner — to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act (SBGG) on legal gender change, i.e. an organised Land-level attempt to make the nationwide self-ID law stricter.

records.name: Berlin
records.current_summary: Berlin remains the German jurisdiction with the deepest anti-discrimination apparatus, the largest visible queer community and the most institutionalised protection infrastructure. Ahead of the 2025 Christopher Street Day (hundreds of thousands expected), organisers explicitly urged participants to "be vigilant" amid a rise in attacks on LGBTQ+ events across Germany, as reported by The Guardian — while the same reporting records that Berlin's and Cologne's parades had not been specifically threatened, the danger falling on smaller towns. The warning is event-specific; everyday institutional reception for a visitor in Berlin is the most hospitable in the country.  National score is 0.71. Berlin sits 0.02 above: the vigilance advisory pulls in a downward direction, but it concerns a single high-profile event, while the standing institutional protections (Land anti-discrimination office, the largest LSBTIQ community infrastructure, the mainstreaming of Pride in the capital) push up. Compared to Bayern (0.67), Berlin has no equivalent public-administration hostility instruction and no legislative-initiative record against the SBGG; compared to the national average, Berlin's additional community infrastructure and enforcement capacity justify the small positive deviation.

sources.claim: The Guardian (26 July 2025) on German Pride parades facing a rise in attacks: Berlin CSD organisers urge vigilance with hundreds of thousands expected; the amadeu-antonio-stiftung counted 55 right-wing-extremist attacks on Pride events nationally in 2024 and 30 so far in 2025 across ~120 parades (including an attack with boiling water), and runs a €100,000 CSD support fund focused on eastern Germany; Maneo, the Berlin anti-violence documentation project, states big-city parades like Berlin and Cologne were not specifically threatened and that smaller towns are hardest to police; a Berlin-Neukölln queer café owner reports 45 police complaints over homophobic attacks in 18 months.

records.name: Brandenburg
records.current_summary: In Cottbus, 20 October 2025, a paper bin was set alight against the wall of the "Regenbogenkombinat" queer cultural centre, damaging the façade; state security (Staatsschutz) opened an arson investigation. The incident sits within a pattern: two venue attacks in the city, year-on-year far-right counter-demonstrations at the CSD (including one organised by "Deutsche Jugend voran"), and a queer community that described itself as "particularly watchful." The subsequent CSD ran under a large police presence with two counter-demonstrations but proceeded without major disruption.  National score is 0.71. Brandenburg sits 0.05 below: the pattern of physical attacks on queer infrastructure (arson, incendiary devices at a housing project) with Staatsschutz involvement meets the "lone incidents barely move a score unless patterned" threshold. Mitigating: police protection was effective and the parade proceeded. Compared to Thüringen (0.65), Brandenburg's threat is concrete and physical; compared to Sachsen (the worst in the dossier with a 700+ neo-Nazi mob at Bautzen), Brandenburg's incidents are smaller in scale and met with a functional institutional response. Compared to Bayern (0.67), Brandenburg's hostility is enacted rather than merely legislative.

sources.claim: LR Online (Cottbus, 21 October 2025, dpa-based): a rubbish container was set alight on the afternoon of Monday 20 October beside the façade of the "Regenbogenkombinat" ("Bunte Welt") queer cultural centre on Thierbacher Straße in Cottbus on the CSD week; nobody was hurt and the fire was out in ~15 minutes, but the Staatsschutz took over the investigation as arson and a political motive cannot be excluded, initiatives call it an attempted firebombing, and the article places it among earlier suspected far-right attacks in the city; two counter-assemblies were registered against the CSD motto "Vereint in Frieden und Vielfalt" and the queer community is described as unusually watchful.

Niederlausitz aktuell report on the Cottbus CSD & Niederlausitz parade (17th edition): it took place under a large police presence with two far-right counter-demonstrations (one organised by "Deutsche Jugend voran") and, despite the tense atmosphere following the Regenbogenkombinat fire, proceeded without major disruption.

records.name: Hessen
records.current_summary: A Hessen Landtag parliamentary inquiry documents that queer-hostile offences recorded by police rose from 33 in 2022 to 83 in 2023, and the same answer reports 135 in 2024 (+52 on the prior year, which the interior minister's reply calls alarming). The dossier flags an irreducible ambiguity: the increases may reflect a real deterioration in safety or a change in police classification practices under the newer BKA LSBTIQ reporting category. No Land-specific trans statute, ordinance or documented event-attack series was found for Hessen beyond this statistical finding; the police have run dedicated LSBTIQ liaison officers in every headquarters since 2010.  National score is 0.71. Hessen sits 0.02 below — the minimum deviation threshold — reflecting a concerning trend whose causality is unresolved. Compared to Bayern (0.67), Hessen lacks any equivalent legislative hostility (no SBGG-initiative participation, no language ban); compared to Berlin (0.73), the statistical signal is the only differentiator and it is caveated. The small deviation treats the trend as a mild negative climate indicator pending confirmation.

sources.claim: Hessen Landtag small inquiry and Interior Minister answer (April 2025): police-registered queer-hostile offences in Hessen rose from 33 (2022) to 83 (2023) and to 135 (2024, +52 year-on-year — described as alarming); notes LSBTIQ* liaison officers established in all police headquarters since 2010 and a framework concept governing them.

Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) situation report on the security of LSBTIQ* people in Germany, published with the Interior Ministry: a multi-year rise in police-registered queer-hostile offences and the new federal reporting category that makes Land-by-Land comparison possible; classification changes can inflate Land counts, so cross-Land numbers need caution.

records.name: Sachsen-Anhalt
records.current_summary: Sachsen-Anhalt co-authored, with Sachsen and Thüringen, a joint Länder Bundesrat initiative (June 2026) to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act (SBGG) in the wake of the "Fall Liebich" — a convicted far-right extremist who had her legal gender changed after sentencing — proposing an abuse-review mechanism defining when registry offices may intervene in gender-marker changes, on the stated ground that self-determination rights are being "abused." The dossier describes critics' view that the initiative would restrict how trans and intersex people use the right; the SPD-led ministries consider the existing law already sufficient. No Land-specific street-attack series, police offence dataset or administrative ban comparable to Bayern's language prohibition was documented for Sachsen-Anhalt in this research pass.  National score is 0.71. Sachsen-Anhalt sits 0.03 below: the SBGG-tightening initiative is a clear legislative-hostility signal but remains an attempt, not an enacted change, and the unit lacks the physical-attack pattern of Brandenburg (0.66) or the equality-dismantling bill of Thüringen (0.65). Compared to Bayern (0.67), Sachsen-Anhalt shares the SBGG-initiative role but has no equivalent standing administrative ban affecting every public counter a visitor encounters.

sources.claim: dpa report (updated 2 June 2026): Sachsen, Sachsen-Anhalt and Thüringen bring a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act, proposing an "abuse review" mechanism with objective, documentable grounds for registry-office intervention, triggered by the Fall Liebich; backed by Union MPs, resisted by the SPD, while the federal family ministry runs a scheduled SBGG evaluation.

records.name: Wales
records.current_summary: Wales's devolved administration publicly maintains an LGBTQ+ Action Plan with a standing update page issued after the For Women Scotland judgment (19 December 2025), and has enacted statutory school guidance ("Rights, Respect, Equality," consultation May 2025) obliging schools to challenge bullying and harassment on gender-reassignment grounds with recording and monitoring, alongside a dedicated national guidance for supporting trans children in development through 2025–26. These measures represent an active state posture of inclusion at a time when the UK-wide EHRC single-sex-services code (in force 5 August 2026) creates a biological-sex facility-exclusion floor identical in Wales to England.  For a visitor the practical risk of service refusal is unchanged — the code binds Welsh facilities as equally as English ones — but the visible institutional commitment (Action Plan maintained, school recording obligations, FOI-disclosed guidance work) shapes policing culture and public discourse. Score sits +0.03 above the national anchor: Wales is not materially safer on facilities, but it is the only devolved administration actively counter-signalling the national climate with published protection programmes. Above England, which has no equivalent positive devolved signal.

Welsh Government statutory school guidance "Rights, Respect, Equality" (consultation May 2025): obliges schools to challenge bullying and harassment on sex, gender-reassignment and sexual-orientation grounds, with incident recording/monitoring and a parental escalation route.

records.name: Victoria
records.current_summary: The Justice Legislation Amendment (Anti-Vilification and Social Cohesion) Act 2025 (No. 11 of 2025, passed April 2025) created both civil and criminal vilification offences and extended protection beyond race and religion to disability, gender identity, sex, sex characteristics, sexual orientation and personal association (Equal Opportunity Act 2010, new Part 6A, s.102B). Victoria is the only Australian jurisdiction where public incitement against a trans person is now a criminal charge, not merely a civil complaint. The Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities 2006 binds public authorities and provides an independent review mechanism absent in NSW, WA and SA.  A Victorian coronial inquest into the deaths of five young transgender women (Bridget Flack, Heather Pierard, Matt Byrne, Natalie Wilson and a fifth identified only as "AS") found Victoria Police failed the search for Flack. Coroner Ingrid Giles issued nine recommendations calling for an overhaul of missing-persons risk assessment for trans people. Advocates characterised the police handling as "a terrible miscarriage of justice." The finding documents a serious institutional failure, but the reform process and the 2025 legislation represent a corrective institutional response that counts as positive evidence under the single-incident and institutional-response rules.  Academic review confirms that Victorian LGBT prison protections are policy-based and not legally enforceable, a cross-jurisdictional weakness.  Vs the national score of 0.86, Victoria sits 0.02 above: the criminal vilification offence is the strongest new legal protection in the country and the Charter adds a structural review mechanism, but the coronial finding on police failure toward a specifically vulnerable sub-population (trans women in sex-work-adjacent contexts) and the thinness of prison policy prevent a larger positive deviation. Vs ACT (0.88), which also has a rights statute and self-ID custody but no equivalent criminal vilification offence and no comparable institutional-failure finding, the two units are at parity from different evidence.

sources.claim: Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission fact sheet explaining the new anti-hate laws: the 2025 Act passed in April 2025 creates civil vilification grounds under the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 (inciting hatred; hateful conduct a reasonable member of the target group would consider hateful) and criminal offences under the Crimes Act; protection extends to disability, gender identity, race, religious belief, sex, sex characteristics and sexual orientation (plus association), with civil grounds commencing 15 April 2026.

ABC News report (29 August 2024) on the Victorian coronial inquest into the deaths of five young transgender women in Melbourne during the pandemic (lead case: Bridget Flack, missing December 2020, died by suicide aged 28): Coroner Ingrid Giles identified multiple Victoria Police failings and made nine recommendations, including urgent investment in trans health care and reform of missing-persons practice; the government is reviewing the recommendations.
